title: Lights dim or flickering
h1: Why are my headlights dim or flickering?
metaDesc: Headlights or dash lights dim or flickering? See if it's the alternator, battery, a loose connection or a bulb, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: lights dim when ac turns on
lights flicker and battery light on
intro: Your lights are a good window into your car's electrical system. Dimming or flickering can be as simple as an old bulb or as serious as an alternator that's about to stop charging. Answer a few questions to narrow down which it might be, and how soon to act.
safety: If the lights keep getting dimmer while you drive, especially at night, pull over somewhere safe before the car loses power.
If you smell burning plastic or see smoke from the dash or under the hood, pull over, turn off the engine and step away from the car.
If the headlights go out completely at night, turn on the hazard lights and get off the road as soon as it's safe.

q_warning.q: Is the battery (charging) warning light on, or are other things acting strange, like gauges jumping or wipers slowing?
q_warning.help: The battery light usually looks like a small red battery with + and − signs. It warns that the car isn't charging, even though it's shaped like a battery.

opts.a: Yes, and the lights keep getting dimmer
Yes, the battery light is on, but the lights look about normal
Lights dim at idle, then brighten when I press the gas
Lights flicker or pulse while driving
Lights dip briefly when something turns on (A/C, windows, brakes)
Only one headlight is dim, flickers or is out
Both headlights are dim all the time, even at speed
Lights are dim mostly with the engine off or when starting

q_flicker.q: What seems to set off the flicker?

opts.a: Bumps, or touching the headlight switch
It started after new LED or HID bulbs were put in
It's a steady pulse that changes with engine speed

result.title: The alternator may have stopped charging, leaving the car running on the battery
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and turn the engine off. Have it towed or call roadside assistance. It may not restart, and the lights could fail.
if: If you can't stop right away, turn off everything you don't need (radio, A/C, heated seats, rear defrost) to stretch the battery until you can pull over.
If you hear a squeal or the temperature gauge rises too, the belt may have broken. Turn off the engine as soon as you're safely stopped.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood or the dash, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: With the battery light on and lights fading, the battery is being drained instead of recharged. Once it runs low, the engine can shut off, and power steering, lights and wipers can all fail with it.

causes.name: Failed alternator
causes.clues: A whining or grinding noise from the engine, or the lights flickered in the days before.

causes.name: Broken or slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal or slap, heavy steering, or the temperature gauge rising.

causes.name: Loose or corroded charging cable
causes.clues: The battery light flickered on and off over bumps before staying on.

you: Once safely stopped with the engine off, look to see if the belt is still on the pulleys.

result.title: The charging system may have a problem. Get it tested right away
result.now: Have the battery and alternator tested as soon as you can, ideally today. Many auto parts stores can test them. Before driving, look at whether the engine belt is still in place (engine off). Until it's tested, turn off electrical extras and avoid driving at night, on highways or far from help.
if: If the lights start dimming or the gauges act up, pull over and have it towed.
If the light only flickered once and went out, it can be a loose connection. Still have the system tested.
If the steering suddenly feels heavy, the temperature gauge rises or you hear a loud squeal, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. The belt may have failed.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: The battery light means the car's computer sees that the system isn't charging properly. The car can run for a while on the battery alone, but how long is hard to predict.

causes.name: Weak or failing alternator
causes.clues: A whining noise, or the lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Slipping or worn belt
causes.clues: A squeal on startup or when turning the steering wheel.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or charging cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the battery terminals, or the light flickers over bumps.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.
Look at the belt for cracks or glazing (engine off).

result.title: The alternator may be getting weak, or the belt may be slipping
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested when convenient. Most auto parts stores offer this.
if: If the battery light comes on or the car becomes slow to start, get it tested within a few days.
If it's slight and only happens with many accessories on, it can be normal on some cars. A test will tell you.
If you smell burning or the lights keep getting dimmer while driving, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: At idle, the alternator spins slowest and makes the least power. A healthy one still keeps up. If the lights dim noticeably at idle and brighten when you rev, the alternator or belt may not be keeping up with demand.

causes.name: Weakening alternator
causes.clues: The dimming has gotten worse over weeks, or there's a whine from the engine.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A brief squeal on cold starts or with the A/C on.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or cranking is slower.

you: Note whether it's worse with the A/C, rear defrost or headlights on high.
shop: Alternator output test at idle and under load

result.title: A pulsing flicker can point to a failing alternator
result.now: Get the charging system tested within the next few days. Keep trips short and avoid night driving if you can.
if: If the battery light comes on or the lights start getting dimmer, pull over and have it towed.
If the flicker changes when you wiggle the battery cables (engine off), a loose connection is more likely.
If you smell burning or the alternator area feels very hot, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving.
result.why: An alternator should give a steady voltage. When parts inside it wear out, the voltage pulses, and you see that as flickering lights that follow engine speed. If the alternator is the cause, it often gets worse until it stops charging, so it's worth testing rather than waiting.

causes.name: Failing alternator voltage regulator or diodes
causes.clues: A whine from the engine, or a battery that keeps going flat.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or ground connection
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on terminals, or the flicker changes over bumps.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal or chirp from the engine.

you: Check the battery terminals for tightness and corrosion.

result.title: A loose connection or worn headlight switch is a common cause
result.now: Check that the battery cables are tight and clean, then book an electrical check when convenient.
if: If the headlights go out completely, even briefly, get it fixed within a day or two and avoid driving at night.
If you smell burning or a connector feels hot, stop using the lights and get it checked right away.
result.why: When bumps or touching the switch make the lights flicker, power is being interrupted somewhere along the way. A worn switch, a loose plug or a corroded ground wire are the usual suspects.

causes.name: Worn headlight switch or stalk
causes.clues: Wiggling the switch makes the lights flicker.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground wire or battery cable
causes.clues: Other things flicker too, like dash lights or the radio.

causes.name: Loose or melted headlight connector
causes.clues: Only one headlight flickers, or the plug looks browned.

you: Gently wiggle the headlight switch with the lights on and see if they flicker.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the lighting and ground circuits

result.title: The new bulbs may not be compatible with your car's electrical system
result.now: Put the original-type bulbs back in and see if the flicker stops.
if: If the flicker stops with the original bulbs, the new ones weren't a match for your car's lighting system.
If it still flickers with the original bulbs, have the wiring and switch checked.
If a bulb connector looks melted or browned, or you smell hot plastic, stop using those lights and have the wiring checked before driving at night.
result.why: Many cars check headlight bulbs by sending small pulses of power through them. Some LED and HID bulbs react to that with flicker, or set off a bulb-out warning. In that case the bulb, rather than the car, is often the issue.

causes.name: Bulb not compatible with the car's bulb-check system
causes.clues: It started right after the new bulbs went in.

causes.name: Loose fit or connector on the new bulb
causes.clues: Only one side flickers.

causes.name: Wiring or switch problem
causes.clues: Other lights flicker too.

you: Reinstall the original-type bulbs and compare.
Check that each bulb is seated and its plug is firmly connected.
shop: Body control module scan for bulb faults

result.title: A brief dip is often normal, but a big one points to the battery or connections
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, and have the battery and charging system tested when convenient.
if: If the dip is getting bigger or the battery light flickers with it, get it tested within a few days.
If the engine stumbles or nearly stalls when the dip happens, get it checked within a day or two.
If the engine actually stalls, stop driving it until it's checked. Steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
result.why: Big electrical loads, like the A/C fan or power windows, briefly pull extra power. A quick, small dip is normal on many cars. A deep or long dip means the battery, alternator or a connection is struggling to keep up.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old.

causes.name: Weak alternator
causes.clues: The lights also dim at idle.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground connection
causes.clues: Several things flicker at once, or it's worse over bumps.

you: Notice which accessory causes the biggest dip.

result.title: Often a bulb on its way out, or a loose bulb connector
result.now: Check that the bulb's plug is firmly connected, then try a new bulb. It's often best to replace both sides so they match.
if: If the new bulb also flickers or is dim, check the connector for melting or browning and have the wiring checked.
If the headlight is completely out, get it fixed promptly. Driving with one headlight is unsafe at night and can get you a ticket.
If the connector or housing smells burnt, stop using that light and have the wiring checked.
result.why: When only one light is affected, the problem is usually at that light: the bulb, its plug or its ground. Bulbs often dim or flicker before they burn out.

causes.name: Aging bulb
causes.clues: The bulb is several years old, or the other side was replaced recently.

causes.name: Loose or corroded bulb connector
causes.clues: The flicker changes if you tap the headlight housing.

causes.name: Moisture inside the headlight
causes.clues: Condensation or water droplets inside the lens.

you: Look for moisture inside the headlight.

result.title: Hazy lenses or aging bulbs are common reasons
result.now: Look at the headlight lenses. If they're yellow or cloudy, clean or restore them. If they're clear and the dash lights look normal, try new bulbs on both sides.
if: If the dash lights are dim too, or the battery is slow to start the car, have the charging system tested.
If it's hard to see the road at night, fix it before driving after dark.
If the lights get dimmer while you drive or the battery light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have the charging system checked before driving further.
result.why: Plastic headlight lenses yellow and cloud with age and sun, which blocks a lot of light. Bulbs also lose brightness over time. Both happen slowly, so you may not notice until it's quite bad.

causes.name: Yellowed or cloudy headlight lenses
causes.clues: The lenses look foggy or yellow from outside.

causes.name: Old bulbs
causes.clues: The bulbs are several years old.

causes.name: Low system voltage or poor ground
causes.clues: Dash lights are dim too, or the battery seems weak.
causes.against: If only the headlights are dim, this is less likely.

you: Compare your headlights with another car's on a wall at night.

result.title: The battery may be weak or not fully charged
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, then have the battery tested. Many auto parts stores offer this.
if: If the car cranks slowly or won't start, try a jump start and get the battery and alternator tested soon.
If the lights also dim while driving, the alternator may be the problem. Get it tested within a few days.
result.why: With the engine off, the lights run only on the battery. If they're dim then but bright once the engine is running, a low or worn battery is a common reason.

causes.name: Aging or weak battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or cold mornings make starting slow.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery terminals
causes.clues: Crusty white or green buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Something draining the battery while parked
causes.clues: It's worse after the car sits for a few days.

you: Look for a date label on the battery.

result.title: Have the battery and charging system tested first
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, then have the battery and charging system tested when convenient.
if: If the battery light comes on or the lights keep getting dimmer, pull over and have it towed.
If only one light is affected, the bulb or its connector is a common cause.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Most dim or flickering light problems come from the battery, alternator, a loose connection or the bulbs themselves. A charging system test is a quick way to check for the more serious causes first.

causes.name: Charging system problem
causes.clues: Lights change with engine speed, or the battery light flickers.

causes.name: Loose or corroded connection
causes.clues: Flickering over bumps.

causes.name: Aging bulbs or hazy lenses
causes.clues: Steady dimness that came on slowly.

you: Note whether it changes with engine speed or over bumps.
